newsitem.title: GERMANY: Foreign investment in Germany "catastrophic" - IW. [CORRECTED 15:15 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Foreign investment in Germany "catastrophic" - IW. [CORRECTED 15:15 GMT]

text.p: The deterrent effect of high wages, excessive company taxes and a lumbering bureaucracy made 1996 the worst year for foreign investment in Germany since World War Two, an economic think-tank said on Tuesday.

Foreign companies withdrew a record net $3 billion (corrects currency from marks) in capital, making Germany the only developed country to record a net outflow of foreign capital, the Institute for the German Economy (IW) said in a report.

On a longer view, net direct foreign investment totalled $17.3 billion from 1991 to 1996 (corrects currency from marks). That was equivalent to a tiny 0.6 percent of total investment in German businesses.
"The catastrophic balance of foreign direct investment results from a fatal mix of high labour costs and business taxes, short working hours and over-regulation," the IW said.

Germany's failure to attract international investors meant that, among developed countries, it outranked only Japan over the past five years in terms of foreign direct investment as a share of total investment. In Japan the figure was just 0.1 percent.
By contrast, foreign investment in European states like Belgium and Luxembourg made up 22.1 percent of the total, in Sweden 17 percent and in Britain 11.7 percent, OECD data show.
Foreign investment in Sweden as a share of the total rose by five times from 1991 to 1996, compared with the previous five years. In Germany it fell by 40 percent.
The IW said Sweden's success as a "magnet" for capital from abroad stemmed from welfare reforms, corporate tax cuts and a reduction of state interference.
"Meanwhile, economic policy in Germany is stuck in a dangerous blockade," the IW commented.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government has tried to battle record post-war unemployment, which it expects to average 4.3 million this year, with a combination of tax reforms, welfare changes and business deregulation.
But the government is backing off from tax-cutting plans after they were blocked by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) in parliament.
Planned pensions reforms are unlikely to cut payroll costs by much and a recent loosening of restrictions on shop opening hours has failed to lift retail sales.
"If the reform backlog is not cleared, we must fear that foreign capital will continue to make a detour around Germany," the IW said.
